question: What if the Mongols had kept riding west in 1242?
short: In spring 1241 two Mongol armies destroyed the Polish and Hungarian hosts within two days, then turned back in 1242. If they had stayed, the likeliest outcome is not a Mongol Paris but a Hungary paying tribute like the Russian principalities, with raids into Austria and Italy that stall at stone walls. West of the Hungarian plain there was not enough grass for a horse army to live on.

divergence.text: The Great Khan Ögedei does not die in December 1241, and the campaign goes on.

plausibility_note: Medium: the death is a coin-flip of history, but the environmental limits on a steppe army in Central Europe do not change.

steps.title: Two armies gone in two days
steps.text: On 9 April 1241 a Mongol wing crushed Henry II of Silesia at Legnica. Two days later Batu and Subutai destroyed King Béla IV's army at Mohi on the Sajó. Hungary was overrun, and Mongol riders reached the Adriatic coast hunting the fleeing king.

sources.cite: Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the West, 1221-1410 (2005)

steps.title: Why they came: the Cumans
steps.text: Part of the motive was punitive. The Cuman leader Köten had fled into Hungary with his people in 1239, and the Mongols treated them as runaway subjects. A campaign to punish a harbouring king is different from a plan to conquer the Atlantic coast.

sources.cite: Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the West, 1221-1410 (2005)

steps.title: The turn back, and a wet spring
steps.text: Ögedei died in December 1241 and Batu withdrew in 1242. The old explanation is succession politics. Tree rings show a cold, very wet spring in 1242 that turned the Hungarian plain to marsh, cutting pasture and making the ground bad for cavalry. Büntgen and Di Cosmo argue that mattered as much as the funeral.

sources.cite: Ulf Büntgen and Nicola Di Cosmo, Climatic and environmental aspects of the Mongol withdrawal from Hungary in 1242 CE, Scientific Reports 6 (2016)

steps.title: The last big pasture
steps.text: The Great Hungarian Plain is the westernmost piece of steppe-like grassland in Europe. Denis Sinor estimated it could feed only a fraction of the horses a Mongol army brought, and past it lie forests, hills, rivers and walled towns. Geography is the strongest brake on this what-if.

sources.cite: Denis Sinor, Horse and pasture in Inner Asian history, Oriens Extremus 19 (1972)

steps.title: Raids that stall at walls
steps.text: With the khan alive, Batu could have wintered in Hungary and raided Austria, Bohemia and Friuli. Mongol armies were superb at sieges in China and Persia with engineers and fodder; in Central Europe they had less of both. The best guess: field victories and burned countryside, but few great cities taken.

steps.title: Hungary as a second Rus
steps.text: The Russian principalities became tributaries of the Golden Horde for about two centuries, ruled by their own princes who fetched patents from Sarai. Hungary on the same footing is the most plausible lasting change: a Catholic kingdom turned toward the steppe, and a weaker eastern shield for Austria and Poland.

sources.cite: Charles Halperin, Russia and the Golden Horde (1985)

steps.title: Plugged into the Mongol world sooner
steps.text: The Mongol peace carried merchants like the Polos, paper money ideas, gunpowder recipes and, later, plague. A Central Europe inside that network might have got all of them faster. This is the most speculative step: it is a direction, not a forecast.

views.name: Juvaini and the old story
views.claim: Batu went home because Ögedei died and a new khan had to be chosen.
views.for: The timing fits, and Mongol princes did gather for elections.
views.against: Batu did not actually attend the kurultai, and the withdrawal began before news could have reached him by some reckonings.

views.name: Büntgen and Di Cosmo
views.claim: A wet, cold spring flooded the plain and starved the horses.
views.for: Tree-ring and documentary evidence for 1242 weather.
views.against: Weather explains a bad season, not a permanent decision.

views.name: Denis Sinor
views.claim: Steppe armies could not live west of the Hungarian plain, so lasting conquest was never on.
views.for: Grassland area and horse numbers; the Golden Horde's border stayed on the steppe edge for centuries.
views.against: Mongols adapted elsewhere, using local infantry and engineers in China and Persia.

unknowns: How many horses the Hungarian plain could actually carry in the 1240s.
Whether Batu planned conquest or only punishment.
How Latin Europe's castles would have held against Chinese and Persian siege engineers.
